Q8166.L1t: Henry Maine was a 19th-century legal historian whose book Ancient Law examined how early legal systems developed.
Q8166.L2t: Maine's phrase appears in Ancient Law, where he contrasts societies organized by family-based status with those organized by individual agreements.
Q8166.L3t: Maine wrote the line as a description of what had happened in the societies he had studied up to then, as the word 'hitherto' signals, and he did not offer it as a rule about what would happen later.
Q8166.L4t: The aphorism is commonly misunderstood because readers treat it as a forecast of future development, when Maine meant it as a description of past change.
Q8166.L2f: Maine published the aphorism in a 1950s essay on the law of contracts, written as a reply to Marxist critics of the legal system.
Q8166.L3f: Maine's own account of status was a loose, shifting one, covering any social position at all, from wealth and occupation to personal taste, which later writers had to narrow down.
Q8166.L4f: The aphorism is mainly misunderstood because readers distort what Maine meant by status, which he defined differently from how it is usually presented.

Q8178.L1t: Both the Roman Empire and Han China were large agrarian empires that expanded through conquest and kept their rule going with professional armies.
Q8178.L2t: Both empires had long trade networks, including the Silk Roads, that linked the Mediterranean world with East and South Asia.
Q8178.L3t: As the overland empires that guarded and funded the Silk Roads broke up, the roads became less safe and less profitable, so merchants turned increasingly to maritime routes across the Indian Ocean.
Q8178.L4t: The collapse of both empires pushed commerce away from the overland Silk Roads and toward Indian Ocean sea routes.
Q8178.L2f: After the Han dynasty fell, Chinese rulers sealed the empire's borders and banned all foreign trade for several centuries.
Q8178.L3f: With both empires gone, the legal codes that had protected women's property and inheritance were abandoned, and the successor states passed laws that took those protections away.
Q8178.L4f: The fall of the two empires led to a decline in the rights of women.

Q8118.L1t: The solar nebula was the cloud of gas and dust that collapsed to form the Sun and the planets about 4.6 billion years ago.
Q8118.L2t: Condensation in the solar nebula depended on temperature, so only metals and rocks could form solids in the hot inner region near the young Sun.
Q8118.L3t: Hydrogen and helium made up about 98 percent of the nebula's mass, which is more than all the heavier materials combined, and of those heavier materials the ices (hydrogen compounds) outweighed the rocks, which in turn outweighed the metals.
Q8118.L4t: Light gases come first by mass, followed by hydrogen compounds, then rocks, and metals come last.
Q8118.L2f: The solar nebula was a perfectly uniform cloud with the same composition at every distance from the Sun, and it did not rotate at all.
Q8118.L3f: Because the ices of water, methane and ammonia were so abundant everywhere, they outweighed even hydrogen and helium together, and the rocks and metals made up the smallest share.
Q8118.L4f: The correct ordering is light gases first, then hydrogen compounds, then metals, and rocks last.
